claim: Postdocs can be known by more than 30 different names, including Visiting Fellow, Research Fellow or Research Associate.
source: These positions provide training, and contribute intellectual capital and a significant workforce, but an analytical view reveals that the ad hoc expansion of such positions is causing problems.

claim: Biomedical research does not respond to classic market forces in the same way as other industries.
source: Although such analyses may seem unnecessary because simple market forces could, in principle, adjust the workforce to meet the needs of the enterprise, biomedical research does not respond to classic market forces in the same way as other industries (Alberts et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alberts et al., 2014

claim: Tracking the outcomes of postdoctoral training accurately has not been performed despite repeated recommendations to do so.
source: An initial step toward this end is to track the outcomes of postdoctoral training accurately (National Academy of Sciences, National Academy of Engineering, and Institute of Medicine, 2014; Polka et al., 2015; Silva et al., 2016) – a task that has not been performed despite repeated recommendations to do so, and which is made more challenging by difficulties in simply defining the postdoc workforce in the first place.
evidence: Supported by citations to National Academy of Sciences et al., 2014; Polka et al., 2015; Silva et al., 2016

claim: The true number of postdocs in the US is uncertain, with recent estimates ranging between 30,000 and 80,000.

evidence: Supported by citations to Heggeness et al., 2016; National Institutes of Health, 2012; Ferguson et al., 2014

claim: For over three decades postdoc numbers have generally increased each year, although the past few years indicate a decline.

claim: There is a labor gap in which supply (the number of postdocs on the job market looking for permanent positions) exceeds demand (the number of positions available).
